name: Jennifer Johnson
chief_complaint: Palpitations and shortness of breath for 6 hours
opening_statement: I've been having this racing feeling in my chest since this morning, and I'm finding it hard to catch my breath, especially when I try to move around.
emotional_baseline: Anxious but cooperative. Concerned about her symptoms but maintains good eye contact and responds appropriately to questions.

symptoms.name: Palpitations
symptoms.onset: 6 hours ago, sudden onset while gardening
symptoms.character: Rapid, irregular, fluttering sensation in chest
symptoms.relieving_factors: None identified, sitting still provides minimal comfort

rag_citations.snippet: Palpitations are the most common presenting symptom in new-onset atrial fibrillation, often described as irregular, rapid, or fluttering sensations

symptoms.name: Dyspnoea
symptoms.onset: Started with palpitations, worsening over past 2 hours
symptoms.character: Shortness of breath at rest, worse with minimal exertion
symptoms.severity: 6/10 - can speak in short sentences only
symptoms.timing: Constant, worse when trying to walk

rag_citations.snippet: Dyspnoea occurs in 40-50% of patients with rapid ventricular response due to reduced cardiac output and ventricular filling time
rag_citations.page_reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial Fibrillation - Clinical Features

symptoms.name: Dizziness
symptoms.severity: 5/10 - has to sit down during episodes
symptoms.timing: 3-4 episodes since onset, particularly when standing

rag_citations.snippet: Presyncope or dizziness may occur with rapid ventricular rates >150 bpm due to compromised cerebral perfusion
rag_citations.page_reference: Cardiovascular > Arrhythmias > Atrial Fibrillation - Rapid Ventricular Response

symptoms.name: Fatigue
symptoms.character: Profound tiredness, unable to perform usual activities

family_history: Father had myocardial infarction at age 72, survived. Mother had stroke at age 75. One sister alive and well, one brother with hypertension. No family history of sudden cardiac death or arrhythmias.

social_history.occupation: Retired primary school teacher (retired 3 years ago)
social_history.alcohol: Occasional glass of wine with dinner (2-3 units per week)
social_history.exercise: Regular walking 30 minutes daily, gardening several times per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband in single-story home, independent with ADLs
social_history.support_network: Strong - husband, two adult children living nearby
social_history.functional_status: Fully independent, active lifestyle until today

general.appearance: Alert, anxious, sitting upright in chair

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP not elevated, no peripheral oedema
cardiovascular.palpation: Apex beat normal position, irregularly irregular pulse at radial artery
cardiovascular.auscultation: Irregularly irregular heart sounds, no murmurs, S1 and S2 vary in intensity, no S3 or S4

respiratory.inspection: Mild tachypnoea, no accessory muscle use
respiratory.auscultation: Bilateral air entry equal, fine bibasal crepitations

examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen soft, non-tender. No focal neurological deficits. Thyroid not enlarged.

ecg.findings: Irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves best seen in V1, ventricular rate 138-152 bpm, QRS normal width, no ST changes
ecg.interpretation: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

blood_tests.fbc: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L, Platelets 245 x10^9/L
blood_tests.uec: Na+ 139 mmol/L, K+ 4.1 mmol/L, Cr 68 µmol/L, eGFR >60 mL/min

investigations.chest_xray: Mild cardiomegaly, no pulmonary oedema, no consolidation
investigations.echocardiogram: To be arranged - urgent outpatient or inpatient depending on management pathway

expected_diagnosis: Atrial Fibrillation (new onset, rapid ventricular response)

expected_management.intervention: Rate control with IV metoprolol or diltiazem
expected_management.rationale: Control rapid ventricular response >140 bpm causing symptoms

expected_management.intervention: Rhythm assessment - consider cardioversion vs rate control strategy
expected_management.rationale: New onset <48 hours, patient may be candidate for electrical or pharmacological cardioversion
expected_management.australian_guideline: eTG recommends cardioversion within 48 hours without anticoagulation if haemodynamically stable

expected_management.rationale: CHA2DS2-VASc = 4 (Age 68=2, Female=1, Hypertension=1) - high stroke risk requires anticoagulation
expected_management.pbs_restriction: DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) or warfarin - PBS listed for stroke prevention in AF

expected_management.rationale: Assess for structural heart disease, valvular disease, left atrial size, LV function
Specialist assessment for long-term rhythm control vs rate control strategy
Continue hypertension and lipid management, lifestyle modification
expected_management.australian_guideline: Heart Foundation guidelines for cardiovascular disease prevention

expected_management.intervention: Patient education - stroke risk, anticoagulation importance, symptom recognition
expected_management.rationale: Ensure understanding of lifelong anticoagulation need and warning signs
expected_management.resource: Heart Foundation AF patient information resources

critical_errors.description: Failure to initiate anticoagulation in patient with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2
critical_errors.consequence: 15-20% annual stroke risk if untreated, immediate patient safety issue

critical_errors.description: Attempting cardioversion without TEE in patient with AF >48 hours duration or unknown onset
critical_errors.consequence: Risk of cardioembolic stroke from left atrial thrombus

critical_errors.description: Failure to control ventricular rate with symptoms of haemodynamic compromise
critical_errors.consequence: Progression to heart failure, syncope, or haemodynamic instability

critical_errors.description: Not checking thyroid function in new-onset AF
critical_errors.consequence: Missing thyrotoxicosis as reversible cause of AF

critical_errors.description: Failure to arrange echocardiogram for structural assessment
critical_errors.consequence: Delayed identification of valvular disease or cardiomyopathy

critical_errors.description: Not documenting time of symptom onset accurately
critical_errors.consequence: Impacts cardioversion decision-making and anticoagulation strategy

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP (Cardiology), Staff Specialist, Royal Adelaide Hospital
fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent case for AMC Clinical Examination preparation. Presents classic new-onset AF with rapid ventricular response in an appropriate demographic. The CHA2DS2-VASc score of 4 correctly emphasizes anticoagulation urgency. Management pathway aligns with current eTG and NHFA/CSANZ guidelines. The critical error regarding cardioversion without TEE is particularly important for candidate safety awareness. Difficulty appropriate for 'Easy' category - straightforward diagnosis with time-critical management decisions.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP (General Medicine), AMC Clinical Examiner, Austin Health
fracp_reviews.comments: Well-constructed case reflecting real-world presentation. The history structure follows SOCRATES appropriately, and the examination findings (irregularly irregular pulse, varying S1/S2 intensity) are pathognomonic. RAG citations correctly reference Australian eTG guidelines rather than international sources. The inclusion of MBS items (16500, 55111, 116) and PBS restrictions adds authentic Australian context. Learning objectives comprehensively cover rate vs rhythm control, CHA2DS2-VASc scoring, and the 48-hour window for cardioversion. Strongly approve for AMC candidate preparation.

learning_objectives.objective: Recognize classic presentation of atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia, affecting 2-4% of population and increasing with age

learning_objectives.objective: Calculate CHA2DS2-VASc score accurately and understand anticoagulation thresholds
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women mandates anticoagulation - reduces stroke risk by 64%

learning_objectives.objective: Differentiate rate control vs rhythm control strategies in AF management
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: RACE II trial showed rate control non-inferior to rhythm control for most patients

learning_objectives.objective: Apply the 48-hour rule for cardioversion in new-onset AF
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Cardioversion within 48 hours does not require prolonged anticoagulation or TEE, but exceeding this window increases stroke risk

learning_objectives.objective: Identify reversible causes of AF using PIRATES mnemonic
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Pulmonary disease, Ischaemia, Rheumatic heart disease, Anaemia, Thyrotoxicosis, Ethanol, Sepsis - addressing these may restore sinus rhythm

learning_objectives.objective: Understand PBS restrictions for DOACs vs warfarin in AF
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: DOACs are PBS-listed for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF, require renal function monitoring

learning_objectives.objective: Recognize haemodynamic instability requiring urgent DC cardioversion
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: Hypotension, acute heart failure, or ongoing ischaemia mandate immediate electrical cardioversion regardless of onset time

learning_objectives.objective: Interpret ECG findings specific to AF (absent P waves, irregularly irregular rhythm, fibrillatory waves)
learning_objectives.clinical_relevance: ECG is diagnostic - distinguishing AF from other arrhythmias guides management and prognosis
